Okay, so I'm trying to figure out which part of an atom would cause it to lose the least mass. The options are losing a proton, a neutron, a nucleus, or an electron. I'm a bit rusty on my physics, but I remember that protons and neutrons make up the nucleus of an atom, while electrons orbit around it. 

First, I think about what each of these particles contributes. Protons are positively charged, and neutrons are neutral. The nucleus is made up of protons and neutrons, right? So if an atom loses a proton, it's losing a part of its nucleus. Similarly, losing a neutron would also affect the nucleus. On the other hand, electrons are much lighter and orbit the nucleus, so losing an electron might not have the same impact.

I recall that in terms of mass, protons and neutrons have similar masses, with neutrons being slightly heavier. Electrons are much lighter, like about 1/1836 of a proton's mass. So losing a proton or neutron would mean losing more mass compared to an electron. But wait, the nucleus itself is made up of multiple protons and neutrons. So if the atom loses a nucleus, that's like losing the entire nucleus, which would be a significant loss of mass.

But the question is about losing one of these things: a proton, neutron, nucleus, or electron. So if you lose a proton, you're removing one part of the nucleus. Similarly, losing a neutron would also remove from the nucleus. Losing the entire nucleus would mean the atom disintegrates, but that's a more drastic change.

I think the key here is that electrons have the smallest mass, so losing one would result in the least mass loss. Protons and neutrons are part of the nucleus, so losing one of those would cause more mass loss than an electron. But wait, when you lose a proton, you're also losing a part of the nucleus, which is more massive. So maybe losing a proton would actually cause more mass loss than losing a neutron because neutrons are a bit heavier.

Wait, no, protons and neutrons are almost similar in mass. A proton is about 1.67e-27 kg, and a neutron is slightly heavier, about 1.675e-27 kg. So losing a neutron would cause a tiny bit more mass loss than a proton. But both are parts of the nucleus, so losing either would affect the overall mass.

But the question is about losing one of these, not multiple. So if you lose a proton, you lose a part of the nucleus, but if you lose a neutron, you also lose a part. However, the nucleus itself is made up of both protons and neutrons. So losing the nucleus as a whole would mean losing all the protons and neutrons at once, which is way more mass than losing one proton or neutron.

So putting it all together, the least mass loss would be from losing an electron because it's the lightest. Then, losing a proton or neutron would be next, but since they're part of the nucleus, maybe losing a neutron causes a tiny bit more loss than a proton. But the options are A) proton, B) neutron, C) nucleus, D) electron.

So the order from least to most mass loss would be D) electron, A) proton, B) neutron, C) nucleus. Therefore, the least is D) electron.
</think>
